title: Paint house
label: idb-list
statement: A row of houses must each be painted red, blue or green, and **no two neighbouring houses may share a colour**. You know what each colour costs for each house. Return the **lowest total cost**.

prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe keep the cheapest total ending in each colour; each house adds its cost to the cheaper of the previous house's other two colours — O(n) time, O(1) memory. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: A row of houses must each be painted red, blue or green, and **no two neighbouring houses may share a colour**. You know what each colour costs for each house. Return the **lowest total cost**.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Exactly three colours? (Yes — the follow-up is k colours.)
- All costs non-negative? (Yes.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Greedy (cheapest colour for each house) breaks as soon as a cheap choice forces an expensive neighbour. Instead, for each house keep three numbers: the cheapest total so far if this house is red, blue or green. Each depends only on the previous house's other two.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "K."eep the cheapest total ending in each colour; each house adds its cost to the cheaper of the previous house's other two colours — O(n) time, O(1) memory."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Greedy choice per house.
- A full n × 3 table when three variables are enough.
- Updating red, then using the NEW red to compute blue — compute all three from the old values first.
